title: Arnold leaves transit post, Scott readies for ‘rodeo,’ Mitchell hangs a shingle, in political notes
summary: Maryland Transit Administration head Holly Arnold steps down after five years, Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott returns to Martha's Vineyard for a fundraiser and former delegate and Hogan administration adviser Keiffer Mitchell returns as a lobbyist, in political notes.
content:
by Christine Condon and Will Hammann, Maryland Matters July 29, 2026

by Christine Condon and Will Hammann, Maryland Matters July 29, 2026

After five years running the agency that runs the state’s trains and buses, Holly Arnold is stepping down.

Arnold, a holdover from the Hogan administration, said her last day as Maryland Transit Administration administrator will be Sept. 1. A successor to run the agency that manages the state’s MARC trains, light rail, subway and bus systems is expected to be named shortly thereafter.

“Serving as MTA Administrator has been the highlight of my career and I am grateful for the opportunity to lead this agency over the last five years,” Arnold said in the statement. “While I will miss the amazing MTA team, I am excited for what the future holds and look forward to spending more time with my family.”

First appointed to the job in 2021 by then-Gov. Larry Hogan, Arnold was reappointed when Gov. Wes Moore took office. During her tenure, the final stretch of track of the planned 16-mile Purple Line light rail was laid recently and the Red Line in Baltimore, killed by Hogan, was revived under Moore. The Washington-area Purple Line is expected to begin service in winter 2027, while ground has yet to be broken on the Red Line, more than 20 years after it was first discussed.

“During her more than 13 years of service with MTA, Administrator Arnold has been a tireless champion for transit, advancing initiatives such as modernizing the light rail, implementing transformative upgrades to the metro subway system, building the Purple Line and infusing a can-do spirit in her work and support of our phenomenal transit employees,” Maryland Department of Transportation Secretary Katie Thomson said in a statement. “We wish her the best in her next chapter.”

Moore said in a statement that, as administrator, Arnold “faced challenges head-on and worked tirelessly to improve service for all riders. Our residents, employers and families have seen the impact of her efforts first-hand, and we are grateful to Administrator Arnold for her diligent service to our state.”

After she leaves office, Arnold’s successor will be appointed by Thomson, with Moore’s approval, according to state law.

“I am proud of what we have accomplished together and am confident the employees and leadership team at MTA will continue to advance the critical projects that will move transit in Maryland forward,” Arnold said.

Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott (D) is returning to Martha’s Vineyard to fundraise for his next reelection race, which won’t start in earnest until 2028.

Scott, who is currently serving his second term in City Hall, made his first fundraising stop at the Massachusetts vacation destination last year, joined by former Baltimore Mayor Stephanie Rawlings-Blake and other Maryland political figures, said Marvin James, a campaign adviser to Scott.

“The mayor has — especially with his appeal as president of the African American Mayors Association — national appeal. There’s been a strong desire for him to go back to the Vineyard,” James said Tuesday.

An online invitation for the Aug. 18 event advertises tickets between $250 and $2,500. Scott’s most recent campaign report, filed in January, showed he had more than $250,000 in the bank.

Officially, the event will focus on Scott’s 2028 reelection bid. But James noted that Scott, who cannot run for a fourth term, has an “open mind” about his political future and job openings that may arise in 2030, including the governor’s mansion, since Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) will not be able to run again.

“This is him getting ready for the rodeo,” James said. “The mayor wants to be ready.”

The vacation town is a popular campaign destination for notable Democrats, including former Vice President Kamala Harris (D) and Moore, who has campaigned there in the past, including in 2023.

Scott cannot run for mayor again in 2032 after city voters in 2022 approved a two-term limit, beginning in 2024, for mayor, comptroller and city council members. The measure, which passed with 71% of the vote, was financially backed by David Smith, the executive chairman of Sinclair Broadcast Group, which owns Baltimore television station Fox 45.

Scott has attracted national attention at times during his tenure leading Maryland’s largest city, including for the city’s rapidly declining homicide rate, and in national television appearances following the collapse of the Francis Scott Key Bridge.

Keiffer J. Mitchell Jr., a former delegate, former Baltimore City Council member and former senior adviser for Gov. Larry Hogan, has a new line for his resume: head of an Annapolis office for Washington-based lobbying firm BGR Group.

BGR announced Monday that Mitchell, currently a vice president of state and local advocacy for the firm, will open an Annapolis office, “strengthening its ability to serve clients before Maryland’s executive branch, General  Assembly, and local governments,” the firm said in a statement announcing the move. It will be the latest state capital office of the company, which also has offices in Atlanta, Phoenix, Nashville and Austin, Texas.

“Keiffer  Mitchell is one of Maryland’s most respected public servants and political professionals,” BGR Group President Erskine Wells said in the announcement. “He and his  family have a distinguished history of service in the state. His experience and credibility in Annapolis  and across the state will help BGR clients understand the issues, build durable relationships, and  achieve results.”

Mitchell’s grandfather, Clarence Mitchell Jr., was a prominent lobbyist for the NAACP and his great-uncle was Rep. Parren Mitchell. An uncle, Clarence M. Mitchell III, served in the General Assembly, as did Clarence M. Mitchell IV. Keiffer Mitchell served on the Baltimore City Council from 1995 to 2007, when he ran unsuccessfully for mayor. He served one term in the House of Delegates, from 2010 to 2014.

Mitchell, a Democrat, then became an adviser to Hogan, a Republican, serving variously as a senior adviser, chief legislative officer and, briefly, as acting chief of staff. He left the Hogan administration in 2022 and joined BGR.

“I am proud to lead BGR’s  expansion in Maryland at a moment when businesses are looking for sophisticated guidance there,”  Mitchell said in the statement from the firm.
